final_candidates.decision_summary: Conservative hydrophobic substitution in the TM region may improve membrane packing and viral fusion, supporting replication fitness.
Conservative stem-helix change preserves hydrophobicity and could stabilize envelope assembly, modestly improving fitness.
Stem-region mutation may enhance folding but the added hydroxyl introduces some risk; retained as a plausible fitness-enhancing variant.

stop_reason.detail: The top-3 ranking appears stable under self-iteration and further introspection would not add objective evidence.

history.rationale: Stem/transmembrane-adjacent substitution can modulate membrane fusion kinetics. This V-to-A change is consistent with epidemic-lineage adaptation and may improve viral replication.
Conservative hydrophobic TM substitution likely improves membrane packing and fusion, supporting replication fitness.
Introducing a polar side chain in the stem helix may stabilize the envelope during entry. This could increase fusion efficiency and overall replication fitness.
Stem-region mutation may stabilize folding, but the introduced hydroxyl adds moderate risk; retained in the top three.
Neutralizing a surface negative charge in domain III could alter host receptor contacts. Improved receptor binding or entry efficiency may enhance replication without major structural disruption.
Removing a charged residue in DIII may alter pH-dependent behavior, but its replication benefit is less certain.
This position is near the N-linked glycosylation motif and may influence glycan exposure or virion incorporation. A smaller hydrophobic side chain could improve viral entry and replication.
Conservative DI substitution is plausible but less clearly linked to fitness than stem/TM changes.
Conservative hydrophobic replacement in the stem region can preserve packing while adjusting flexibility. This may support efficient membrane fusion and improved viral fitness.
Conservative stem-helix substitution preserves hydrophobicity and may stabilize envelope assembly; moved above A410T.
The charge change at a domain interface may strengthen protein contacts during low-pH structural rearrangements. Improved fusion competence can directly benefit replication.
Charge-changing mutation could affect fusion-related interactions but carries higher stability risk; keep as a backup.
Adding a methyl group on a domain III surface loop may slightly increase receptor-binding contact surface. This could enhance cell attachment and downstream replication.
Conservative DIII substitution is possible but not strongly supported by replication-related reasoning.
Removing a surface hydroxyl in domain III may reduce deleterious polar clashes while preserving the overall fold. The altered surface could improve entry efficiency.
Removing a DIII hydroxyl could alter local contacts; rank lowered because of neutral destabilization risk.
Replacing a polar residue in the membrane-proximal region with alanine may improve hydrophobic matching with the lipid bilayer. This can enhance assembly and infectious particle production.
TM polar-to-alanine change is conservative but has unclear fitness benefit; lowest priority in the current pool.
A polar addition in the stem segment could stabilize the elongated hairpin required for fusion. Enhanced post-fusion stability may increase replication fitness.
Nearby stem polar mutation may be tolerated but is less likely to improve fitness than A410T.
